title: How would you design a search service (e.g. product/catalog search) — why NOT run full-text search as `LIKE '%...%'` against the primary DB, how a dedicated engine (Elasticsearch/OpenSearch/Solr) uses an inverted index for millisecond retrieval with ranking/relevance, typo tolerance (fuzzy), filtering/sorting/pagination, and how do you keep the search index in sync with the source of truth (asynchronous indexing via events/CDC, accepting eventual consistency)?
shortTitle: How would you design a search service with an inverted index instead of LIKE queries

s1_definition.profdef: A search service answers free-text queries by maintaining a dedicated full-text engine such as Elasticsearch, OpenSearch, or Solr built on an inverted index, rather than running `LIKE '%term%'` against the primary transactional database. The inverted index maps each token to the list of documents containing it, enabling millisecond retrieval with relevance ranking, fuzzy typo tolerance, filtering, sorting, and pagination. The relational database remains the source of truth, and the index is kept in sync asynchronously through domain events or change data capture, accepting eventual consistency in exchange for fast, rich search that does not load the primary database.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India has a huge filing room of transactions and products for customers like Rajesh and Priya. If someone asks "find every record mentioning home loan", a clerk using LIKE would read every single file cover to cover, every time, which is painfully slow once there are millions of files. Instead the bank keeps a separate index card catalog (inverted index) where under the word "loan" there is a card listing exactly which files contain it. Now a lookup is instant. The master files stay in the vault (database), and whenever a file changes, a runner updates the catalog shortly after (asynchronous sync), so the catalog is almost always current, just a moment behind.
s1_definition.oneliner: Don't scan the primary DB with LIKE; keep a dedicated inverted-index engine updated asynchronously from events, so search is millisecond-fast with ranking and typo tolerance while the DB stays the source of truth.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A search service answers free-text queries by maintaining a dedicated full-text engine such as Elasticsearch, OpenSearch, or Solr built on an inverted index, rather than running `LIKE '%term%'` against the primary transactional database. The inverted index maps each token to the list of documents containing it, enabling millisecond retrieval with relevance ranking, fuzzy typo tolerance, filtering, sorting, and pagination. The relational database remains the source of truth, and the index is kept in sync asynchronously through domain events or change data capture, accepting eventual consistency in exchange for fast, rich search that does not load the primary database.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India has a huge filing room of transactions and products for customers like Rajesh and Priya. If someone asks "find every record mentioning home loan", a clerk using LIKE would read every single file cover to cover, every time, which is painfully slow once there are millions of files. Instead the bank keeps a separate index card catalog (inverted index) where under the word "loan" there is a card listing exactly which files contain it. Now a lookup is instant. The master files stay in the vault (database), and whenever a file changes, a runner updates the catalog shortly after (asynchronous sync), so the catalog is almost always current, just a moment behind.

**One line to remember:** Don't scan the primary DB with LIKE; keep a dedicated inverted-index engine updated asynchronously from events, so search is millisecond-fast with ranking and typo tolerance while the DB stays the source of truth.

sections.s2_technical:
Why not LIKE against the primary database. A query like `WHERE description LIKE '%home loan%'` has a leading wildcard, so no B-tree index can be used and the database performs a full table scan, reading every row. On a few thousand rows it is fine; on millions it is slow and gets slower as data grows. Worse, it runs on your primary transactional database, competing for CPU, memory, and IO with the account updates and transfers that actually must be fast and consistent. A handful of heavy search queries can degrade the whole bank's core operations. LIKE also cannot rank by relevance, cannot tolerate typos, and handles multi-word and partial matches poorly. It is the wrong tool for full-text search.

How an inverted index works. A dedicated search engine tokenizes each document into terms, lowercases, removes stop words, and stems them (so "loans" and "loan" match), then builds an inverted index: a map from each term to a posting list of the document IDs that contain it, often with term frequencies and positions. To answer "home loan", the engine looks up the posting list for "home" and for "loan" and intersects or unions them, which is a direct lookup rather than a scan, so it returns in milliseconds even across millions of documents. This is the opposite of a database row scan: instead of "for each document, does it contain the term", it is "for each term, which documents have it".

Ranking and relevance. Search is not just match-or-not; results are ordered by how relevant they are. Engines use scoring like BM25, which rewards documents where the query terms are frequent and rare across the corpus, so a product whose title is exactly "Home Loan" ranks above one that merely mentions it in passing. You can boost fields (title matches count more than description), apply recency boosts, and tune relevance, which LIKE simply cannot do.

Typo tolerance (fuzzy). Users mistype. Fuzzy matching uses edit distance (Levenshtein) so "hoem lon" still finds "home loan" within an allowed number of character edits. The engine supports this natively, and you tune the fuzziness so it is forgiving without being noisy.

Filtering, sorting, pagination. Real search combines a text query with structured filters: "home loan products with interest rate under 9% sorted by rate, page 2". The engine applies the full-text match, then filters on numeric and keyword fields, sorts, and paginates efficiently, typically with search-after cursors for deep pagination rather than large offsets. This rich query model is built in.

Keeping the index in sync with the source of truth. The database remains authoritative; the index is a derived, searchable copy. You never write only to the index. Two common sync approaches: event-driven, where the service that updates a product also publishes a domain event like ProductUpdated that an indexing consumer applies to the search engine; and change data capture (CDC), where a tool like Debezium reads the database's transaction log and streams every change to an indexer, which requires no application code changes and never misses a write. Both are asynchronous, so there is a short lag between a database write and the index reflecting it. This is eventual consistency: search results may be a second or two stale, which is perfectly acceptable for catalog search and far cheaper than keeping them perfectly synchronous.

Handling failures and reindexing. The async pipeline must be reliable: failed index updates retry, and a dead letter queue captures ones that cannot be applied. You also keep the ability to rebuild the entire index from the source of truth, because indexes get corrupted or schemas change, and a full reindex from the database is your recovery path. You often index into a new index and atomically swap an alias to it for zero-downtime reindexing.

The senior nuance is that search and the primary store have different shapes. The database is normalized for correct writes; the search index is denormalized and flattened for fast reads, often duplicating data from several tables into one document. You deliberately accept that duplication and the eventual consistency it implies, because the two systems optimize for opposite goals, writes versus search.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India has a product and transaction catalog. Customers like Rajesh (SAV2001) and Priya (CUR3001) search for products ("home loan", "fixed deposit") and their own transaction history by free text.

Problem 1 — search ran LIKE on the core database and slowed everything. During a campaign, thousands of product searches used LIKE '%...%', forcing full table scans that competed with live transfers, and the whole system slowed. This is why we move search off the primary DB onto a dedicated inverted-index engine.

Problem 2 — typos returned nothing. A customer searching "houm loan" got zero results even though "home loan" existed. This is why we need fuzzy typo tolerance, which an inverted-index engine provides but LIKE cannot.

Problem 3 — after a product's rate changed, search showed the old rate. The index was updated manually and drifted from the database. This is why we sync asynchronously from events or CDC so the index stays current with the source of truth, accepting a short eventual-consistency lag.

The mini-project builds a runnable demo of a mini inverted-index search engine: a `Product` document, an `InvertedIndex` with tokenization and posting lists, BM25-style scoring, fuzzy matching by edit distance, filtering and pagination, and an event-driven `IndexSyncConsumer` that keeps the index updated from ProductUpdated events. It indexes loan and deposit products and runs ranked, fuzzy, filtered searches.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build
mvn clean package -DskipTests

# Run the mini search-engine demo
java -cp target/catalog-search-service-1.0.0.jar com.bank.search.SearchDemo

# Run the service (fronting OpenSearch)
java -jar target/catalog-search-service-1.0.0.jar

# Search the API
curl "http://localhost:8080/api/v1/search?q=home%20loan&maxRate=9.0&page=0&size=10"

# Zero-downtime reindex: build products-v4 then swap the alias
curl -X POST https://opensearch.nbi.local:9200/_aliases \
  -d '{"actions":[{"remove":{"index":"products-v3","alias":"products"}},{"add":{"index":"products-v4","alias":"products"}}]}'
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: four products indexed; queries "home loan", the typo "houm lon", a filtered "loan" under 9%, and an async rate update.

Step 1: Each product is tokenized. "Home Loan" becomes terms home and loan. The inverted index stores home to {P1,P2} and loan to {P1,P2,P3}. This happens once at index time, not per query.

Step 2: Query "home loan" tokenizes to home and loan. The engine looks up the posting lists directly, no table scan. P1 and P2 contain both terms and score highest; P3 contains only loan and scores lower. Results come back ranked: P1, P2, then P3.

Step 3: Query "houm lon" tokenizes to houm and lon, which are not exact terms. The fuzzy matcher computes edit distance: houm to home is 1 edit, lon to loan is 1 edit, both within the limit of 2, so they match the same posting lists. The typo still returns the home loans, something LIKE could never do.

Step 4: Query "loan" with a filter rate under 9.0 matches P1, P2, P3 by text, then applies the structured filter, dropping P3 (12.5) and keeping P1 (8.5) and P2 (8.9), sorted by score and paginated.

Step 5: The product P1's rate changes to 8.25 in the database. The service publishes a ProductUpdated event; the IndexSyncConsumer applies it asynchronously, re-indexing P1. A moment later, searching "home loan" shows P1 with the new rate 8.25. Between the DB write and this sync there was a brief lag, which is the accepted eventual consistency.

Final output:

```

2026-10-24 15:47:03 [INFO   ]   P2 "Home Loan Plus" rate=8.90 score=...
```

sections.s5b_flow:
```
  ── Indexing (write path, asynchronous) ──
  Product DB (source of truth)
    │ UPDATE products SET rate=8.25 WHERE id=P1
    ▼
  CDC (Debezium) / domain event ProductUpdated
    │ Kafka db.products.changelog
    ▼
  IndexSyncConsumer.onProductUpdated()
    │ tokenize → update posting lists
    ▼
  Inverted Index (home→{P1,P2}, loan→{P1,P2,P3})
     (eventual consistency: index lags DB by ~1s)

  ── Search (read path, millisecond) ──
  Query "houm lon"
    │ tokenize → [houm, lon]
    │ fuzzy: houm≈home (1 edit), lon≈loan (1 edit)
    ▼
  posting lookup (NO table scan)
    │ home→{P1,P2}  loan→{P1,P2,P3}
    │ score BM25, apply filter rate<9, sort, paginate
    ▼
  Results: P1, P2 (ranked)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
I never implement full-text search as a LIKE with leading wildcards against the primary database, and the reason is both performance and isolation. A LIKE percent-term-percent cannot use any B-tree index, so the database performs a full table scan reading every row, which is fine on thousands of rows but slow and worsening on millions, and critically it runs on the same transactional database that must keep account updates and transfers fast and consistent, so a handful of heavy search queries degrade the whole bank's core operations. On my project at National Bank of India this is exactly what happened during a campaign, product searches on LIKE slowed live transfers, which is why we moved search onto a dedicated engine.

A dedicated engine like Elasticsearch, OpenSearch, or Solr is built on an inverted index. At index time it tokenizes each document, lowercases, removes stop words, and stems, then stores a map from each term to a posting list of the document IDs containing it. To answer a query it looks up the posting lists for the query terms and intersects or unions them, which is a direct lookup rather than a scan, so it returns in milliseconds even across millions of documents. On top of that it ranks results by relevance using scoring like BM25, which rewards documents where the query terms are frequent and rare across the corpus, so an exact title match ranks above an incidental mention, and I can boost the title field over the description. It also gives fuzzy typo tolerance through edit distance, so a search for houm lon still finds home loan, which LIKE could never do, and it handles structured filtering, sorting, and efficient pagination natively.

The key architectural discipline is keeping the index in sync with the source of truth. The relational database stays authoritative and the index is a derived, denormalized, searchable copy, so I never write only to the index. I sync asynchronously, either with domain events where the service that updates a product publishes a ProductUpdated event that an indexing consumer applies, or with change data capture where a tool like Debezium streams every database change from the transaction log to the indexer with no application code and no missed writes. Both are asynchronous, so there is a short lag between a database write and the index reflecting it, and I consciously accept that eventual consistency because catalog search being a second or two stale is harmless and far cheaper than perfect synchrony. This is what fixed our stale-rate problem.

I also build the pipeline to be reliable and recoverable: failed index updates retry into a dead letter queue, and I keep the ability to rebuild the entire index from the database, which I do by indexing into a new index and atomically swapping an alias for zero-downtime reindexing. The deeper point I make is that the database and the search index optimize for opposite goals, the database is normalized for correct writes while the index is denormalized and flattened for fast reads, so I deliberately duplicate data into the search document and accept the eventual consistency that implies.

The one-line summary I give an interviewer is that I keep search off the primary database on a dedicated inverted-index engine that gives millisecond ranked, fuzzy, filtered, paginated results, I keep the database as the source of truth, and I sync the index asynchronously through events or change data capture, accepting eventual consistency in exchange for fast, rich search that never loads the transactional store.
